pitch_detail.notes: Pick the right-most of the three cracks on the south wall, tucked beside the corner. A short run of hand jams turns into an offwidth lasting a couple of metres, after which the crack gives hand jams, ring locks and finger locks of good quality. Then move right onto the easier-angled hand crack and follow it to a slanted ledge, the first belay.
Go straight up the vertical cracks to the next ledge, shift right into a hand crack and keep climbing directly. The angle is easy apart from the start and one short steeper section midway.
Wander around the highest smokestack onto its east side, then follow a hand crack to the top. Descend by rappelling off slung blocks.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches matching the stored count. Text gives no per-pitch grades, lengths or bolt counts, so none written. Rappel is only 'slung blocks', no station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Spring ski approach noted (ice in cracks, ice axe handy); not stored here.

pitch_detail.notes: Reaching the start ledge may need an extra short pitch or a dirty solo, and the ledge is covered in loose rock. Begin in the flare's rear crack and pull over a bulge. From there, take either the wider cracks above (easier) or a stemming corner down and to the left that needs micro gear and heavy cleaning. Belay on a bolted anchor under the big left-facing corner. Graded 5.10, possibly with a plus.
Wide cracks run up the left-facing corner to a ledge, where a gear belay takes pieces of 1 to 2 inches.
A few metres of wide climbing lead up the right-facing corner, then a hand crack goes to a ledge with a large slung horn. Pieces #4 and #5 are useful on this and the previous pitch.

Pull the bulge above the belay (a 4 or 5 inch piece still helps), then work up ledges, eventually cutting back right. At a chimney, downclimb about 3 m on good cracks, protecting the second, and climb up a short way to a gear belay stance. Rock on this pitch is the weakest of the route.

Excellent hand and finger cracks lead up and slightly left, then a few exciting moves gain a right-facing lieback corner. Follow that to a ledge just beneath the overlap, where a gear belay is needed. Sustained and rewarding.
Hard moves pull over the overlap into a groove. Place gear, then exit left onto the face rather than continuing up the dirty corner. Somewhat runout face climbing reaches a two-bolt belay.

Go up and left past gear and one bolt to twin seams splitting the golden face. Thin moves with tiny gear lead to a commitment to the left-hand crack, which you follow to a bolted anchor beneath the obvious roof.

Climb to the roof and pull it, the crux, then make a tricky crack switch shortly after to easier cracks out right, ending at another bolted anchor. Sustained 5.10 and 5.11 with lots of micro gear and some runouts. The line over the roof reaches the top of the pillar; the usual way off is rappelling from slings.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with grade, length, anchors where stated. Unlisted approach pitch to the start ledge mentioned in P1. Rappel is described only as 'rap the route, two 60 m ropes, not every anchor at a belay' - no station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored descent text agrees (two ropes, loose rock, rope snags). Source says P1 could be 5.10+; stored grade 5.11+ matches P8.

pitch_detail.notes: A ramp leads into steep, juggy, broken cracks and flakes that end at a big ledge under a slab trending left.
Cross the slab, then work through corners and roofs, drifting right toward a golden crack. P1 and P2 loosely follow an older line.

A wide crack trending right leads to a 5.10 mantle, then the line cuts back left to the golden crack splitting the wall. Rope drag and protecting the follower on the slab move pull against each other, so back-clean as needed. A finger crack goes through a small roof, followed by a perfect thin hand crack to a decent ledge. Uses .75 and 1 cams, then 3 and 4 near the top; stoppers make a good belay.
Take the crack up and left into a left-facing corner and stop on the first good ledge.

Step up and left from the belay to a splitter crack that angles up and right, avoiding the choss flakes out left. It passes an overlap, then continues up a right-leaning crack with slabby footholds to a large ledge. Sling a big block there and keep rocks off your partner.
An easy ramp past big blocks leads to two steep corners, trending right, then another big ledge.
Go straight into a thin technical corner, then work up blocky ground trending left. Belay under the steep cracks that lead to the summit.

Move right across the belay ledge and stem from a detached pillar to enter cracks and a wide slot that lead to the summit. The descent is by rappel down the bolted stations of the west face, using two ropes.

review.changed: Wrote all 8 pitches with grade and length. Rappel is 'bolted stations on the west face with two ropes' with no per-station list, so no rappel table. P3 marked crux as the only 5.11- reached outright with a bolder description; P5 also 5.11-.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.11- matches; stored length null (pitch lengths sum to about 355 m).

pitch_detail.notes: Start at the top of the snowfield, or in the moat later in the season. Follow the groove or crack up and right; where the crack divides in two, a bolt sits about 8 ft up on the right, and that bolt plus a fixed nut forms the belay.
Follow a broken crack angling left toward a clean break in the overlap. Belay at two bolts just beneath steeper rock and the next weakness.

Climb the grassy groove crack above the belay, slinging an alder and placing small gear, and watch for loose blocks. A careful move gets through the steep section, then a wide crack takes #2 to #5 cams. Belay at a small alcove above the offwidth.
Go straight up the grassy crack, finding chockstones, and clip three bolts near the top of the pitch.

Climb the vegetated groove and clip two bolts. When the groove gets bushy, a bolt appears out right on the green slab. Between there and the next bolt the climbing is runout with no gear, then return to the groove for more protection. The pitch ends at a bolted anchor.
Follow the groove, taking gear where you can, clip a bolt, then step right and up to the bolted anchor.
Leave the groove to the right and ramble up low fifth-class terrain with some gear and a single bolt. Stop in the dark alcove, with steeper ground and a large tree above. A full rope stretch.
Stem up the dark alcove with gear, then move onto the face through rotten rock to the belay, passing three bolts and some gear. The belay is at a tree.
Two more bolts, gear and big chockstones protect a chimney with several steps, ending at a two-bolt belay in another alcove.
Place gear in the slot above the belay, finishing at a bolt near the top beside some loose rock.
Poor rock here: go up the crumbling arete on the left side of the weakness, passing one bolt, then two more bolts, and expect more loose stone.
Climb the shallow weakness on its left side past two bolts, a rappel station and trees to a sling. Belay from Heather ledge, passing the rappel station.
From Heather ledge, go past a small hemlock and onto the arete, past two bolts and some gear, to the feature summit. The two-bolt anchor sits just under the high point.

review.changed: Wrote all 13 pitches. Only P3 and P9 carry a grade (5.10a), no crux flagged because two pitches share it. Rappel stations are mentioned but not listed station by station, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10a R and 13 pitches agree; total of pitch lengths is about 650 m vs stored 640.

pitch_detail.notes: A thin crack leads to a small roof under 10 m up. Pull through it, climb the slight corner to reach a dyke, and belay at the two-bolt anchor.
Follow the dyke, angling right under a steeper section of wall, and stop at the foot of a short dihedral that faces left.
Bolted face climbing leads left over odd granite pods and chicken heads. A cruxy last move reaches an anchor just around the corner to the left.
From the belay, cross the face to the right to reach the prominent corner.

Stem up the corner, using hand jams in the moss for about 15 m, then step out right onto the steep face. Adventurous climbing between well-spaced bolts leads to the base of a crack, which gets better as it goes and ends in a hand crack as the angle eases.
Layback the corner on the right, then step back left across a slab to the anchor. It can be linked with P5 as a 70 m rope-stretcher.

Slab climbing trends up and right to a thin seam with bolts. Most moves are 5.11, and a three-bolt ladder bypasses two of them; these might go free at 5.11+ or 5.12-. A slightly dirty thin crack follows.
A line of bolts heads up and left to a right-facing corner. The anchor hangs under a roof that bulges above.
Cross left past two bolts and climb mixed corners. About 40 m up you reach a grassy arete; scramble to the right and up to a bolted anchor on a small vertical wall.

The angle lessens and short climbing bursts alternate with heather scrambling. Go around a small pinnacle on its right, then cross heather leftward with a hard traverse to a bolted belay beneath a roof.
Take the vegetated gully on the right, then find the easiest line up another overgrown corner. Easy, runout face climbing then drifts right to a bolted anchor.
Work around to the right and up a small groove into a second chimney-like groove holding a bolt. Belay before the string of big blocky boulders.
Scramble heather left toward a vegetated splitter hand crack with a very short 5.10- section. Cross right to another short crack. The belay bolts are on the vertical wall.
Diagonal cracks, back and forth, lead to the gendarme visible from camp.
Heather and an unprotected slab lead to the final anchor at the top.

review.changed: Wrote all 15 pitches with stated grade, bolts and lengths; anchor given only where noted. Rappel advice is general (2x70 m, skip gear belays, one specific detour from P6 to the P4 anchor), not a station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11- A0, 15 pitches agree. Stored length 604 m vs sum of stated pitch lengths about 625 m.

pitch_detail.notes: Skip the loose chimney on the left and climb easy solid rock to its right, a short pitch to the foot of the wall. The chimney can be downclimbed on the descent.

Three cracks mark this part of the wall on the right side. The route takes the middle one, since the right was wet and the left looked wider. A questionable chockstone sits about three quarters of the way up. The pitch is steeper than it looks, sustained throughout, and ends at a hanging stance on two bolts. Probably 5.11a; protection is awkward in places.

Easy climbing with no gear for the first 15-20 ft leads up and left to a large ledge system. Step left onto a slab and corner and climb about 50 ft more to a pile of large flakes and blocks. Tiptoe around the right side into a sustained left-facing corner, the crux of the pitch, and belay at its top in big cracks taking #3 and #4 cams.
Mostly easy cracks and flakes lead up and right beneath roofs. Climb to the roofs, then step straight right to a good ledge system and belay.

Keep heading right on moderate ground to another corner system that faces left. The first 20 ft are mossy and dirty, then it cleans up and eases. Quest generally upward, bending right and finally left, to belay over a rubble-covered ledge. The rappels start right at the face's edge.

rappel_detail.notes: Starts slightly to the left of the line you climbed. Steep rappel back to the ledge where P5 began.
Straight down and slightly right. Keep some momentum to stay in contact with the steep wall.
A gently overhanging wall takes you to the base of P1, still about 20 m above the glacier in August; it may be closer earlier in the season.

review.changed: Wrote 5 pitches (lengths approximate, as stated) and a 4-station rappel table. Below rap 4, downclimb; a natural quartzite thread near the base of P1 could serve as an extra rappel anchor. Rappel lengths are estimates. (Reviewer: estimated rappel lengths removed.)
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11 PG13 and 5 pitches agree. Two ropes needed; an alternative is 3rd/4th class to the summit.

pitch_detail.notes: The flagging tape stops roughly 20 ft above the treeline on the scree, and the start is right there; if you find yourself scrambling you overshot. A brief easy section is followed by scrambling to an anchor. Pitches 1-3 can be skipped by 4th-class scrambling to the right for those solid unroped.
Some technical moves reach a ramp that leans right. A directional bolt sits on the ramp; clip it, then scramble over to the anchor on the climber's right.
Pleasant climbing on good bolts, then a short scramble to the next anchor.

Start a little left of the anchor, taking the easiest ground to the first bolt. Hard moves cross the overhang, with interesting climbing above. Two sections of broken rock need care. Finish by topping out on the pillar. From the start of this pitch you can scramble the gully to the climber's left to reach other routes.
This is the best pitch. An open book leaning left rises from the top of the pillar, with steady difficulty at the grade, relying on careful footwork and balance. Extendable slings help with drag.

review.changed: Wrote all 5 pitches with grade and length. Rappel the route is mentioned without stations, so no rappel table.

pitch_detail.notes: Harder than it looks, with careful balance needed. If scrambling up from below, the anchor is out of sight on the easiest line; undercling right from the rocky gully (about 5.0). The belay is to the right, just under the large white block.

Follow the obvious crack starting about 4 ft right of the anchors, and after 10 m go straight on past it through small roofs and block-like bits with a few good gear options. The first bolt is around 15 m up and visible from the belay; hard climbing begins there. The lower part takes a single rack, no harder than 5.10b.
A few difficult moves remain on this last pitch. There is a slight runout between the second and third bolts.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches. Anchors not explicitly typed beyond P1/P2 so omitted.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11b/c and 3 pitches agree; the second pitch is currently only partly bolted.

pitch_detail.notes: The climb starts right of a gully; avoid wearing away the belayer's built-up platform. Despite the friendly angle, it is pumpy and hard, with a cruxy roof right at the start. A line of bolts leaning right leads to anchors on a small ledge.
This is the same as the second pitch of Ticks Flying Everywhere.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Rappel back to Goat Ledge is stored; no station list.
review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10d, but the text rates the first pitch 5.11a and the second 5.10b, so the route's top grade is 5.11a.

pitch_detail.notes: Identical to the first pitch of Entourage Effect.
From the second anchor, shared with Entourage Effect, follow bolts left, with climbing that gets steadily harder as you move out onto the face.

Sustained and challenging. After about five bolts, veer sharply right to dodge the hard roof. Roughly 10 m up, cut well over to the right across tan-brown stone where the next bolts are, climb a few metres more, then work back left and mantle over the roof band. Three more bolts later, a loose-looking but solid corner leads left to a bolt just over the roof; finish up and left. A harder straight-up variation has studs but no hangers. Extendable draws keep rope drag down.

review.changed: Wrote all 3 pitches. Rappel descent not listed per station.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11b and 3 pitches agree. P3 notes bolt counts as uncertain.

pitch_detail.notes: The terrain changes a lot, and one tricky offwidth section calls for fist jams.
From the anchors, keep low as you traverse left, then enjoy mixed face moves leading to a demanding arete. Join the final few metres of Crystalline to top out.

review.changed: Wrote both pitches. Rappel back to Goat Ledge, or top out on Crystalline and walk off; no station list.

pitch_detail.notes: Access it by following a narrow ledge that runs right from the large tree on Goat Ledge. Good rock and excellent climbing, with the belay at an anchor slightly left.
Tricky moves through the corner system, then an exposed step right onto the arete before topping out.

review.other_findings: Stored grade 5.10c, but the harder pitch is described as 5.10b.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb straight up to a bolt at about 15 ft, then move left at a steep juggy section protected by two bolts; this is the crux.
Go up over a small wall to a right-facing corner, then shift left onto the arete face past a bolt, and continue up and right to a crack in a slab. Two-bolt anchor.

Start up rock just right of the belay to reach fourth-class dirt and grass, then angle up left along a wall and through a short steep boulder problem with conifer branches. After the anchor, hike left and up a goat path circling above the P2 anchor to a two-bolt rap station.
Go up and left to a slab with a pretty dike and a single bolt, follow the dike up left to a distinct long tree branch, and climb that to a two-bolt anchor on a small ledge.
Climb up and right toward a left-slanting slab with a bolt. Work leftward up the slab to a small alcove ledge with a two-bolt belay.
Straight up, then leftward over small arete features to a good ledge and a two-bolt belay.
Head up left past a tree beside a gully, then right near the top to a good ledge with a two-bolt belay.
Climb to a large rock ledge; the two-bolt anchor is on the wall at its rear.
Move left off the ledge and head up toward a clump of conifers with a two-bolt anchor.

Pass a bolt to a corner that faces left, climb straight up it to heather meadows, then scramble up to the anchor, a pair of bolts on a small vertical face higher up. From here an easy goat path with cairns and flagging leads to Crossover Pass.

review.changed: Wrote all 10 pitches. Descent is rapping the route with a single 60 m rope from rings and mailons, but stations are not listed one by one, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.7, 10 pitches agree. Landslide debris and rockfall on the approach.

pitch_detail.notes: Start about 5 m right of the foot of the Elephant Trunk pillar, in a short 5.11- splitter finger crack rising from the glacier. It leads to the right end of a little overlap, which is passed with a short wide layback at 5.11. Continue in a very shallow right-facing crack, then move left to the next crack and follow that to the bolted belay (also 5.11).

Take the crack right of the piton belay and use face moves left of it to reach the first small roof's right side. A hand crack in the right-facing corner goes to the roof, which you cross leftward, then follow a crack bending slightly right (pitons) to the steep finger crack. The final 4 m make up the crux, easily aided at C1 if needed. The belay is bolted.
A long corner above, with a bolted belay at 60 m. You can break it into two shorter pitches at any of the good stances, several of which hold old pitons.
A sustained, enduro corner leads to the top of the Elephant Trunk pillar. One old quarter-inch bolt is also found there. Extra medium cams help.

Step left from the belay to an old aluminum self-drive, then trend right on thin cracks and face moves to a ramp rising right. Place gear in the crack at the ramp's top, climb the face first left, then back right to the crack 5 m up. Belaying here, or below the big roof a few metres on, is an option. Above, the left-facing corner goes 30 m and the roof can be broken at only 5.9, ending on a poor hanging slab stance.

Skip the dirty left-facing corner and cross right along a face crack to a fine, clean 5.8 hands-and-fists crack that leaves the main corner. Follow it (old quarter-inch bolt) until good ledges and cracks let you move up the face. Many places to belay. Length is 30-40 m.

A somewhat dubious pitch, recommended as two 30 m pitches. Go up left toward a small 5.8 overlap onto a little pillar about 30 m out; a belay there reduces drag. From the pillar, improvise a line across and left to an alcove belay at the 60 m mark, right above the cracks coming from the slab belay over P5. Route-finding can be vague, and old wooden blocks and pins dot the pitch.
Take the left-hand crack until it becomes a shallow, low-angle crack facing left. Build an anchor on the ledge sitting just over an old quarter-inch bolt.

Trend left past a series of corners facing left, then go straight up to a stance under a big black overhanging corner that faces right. Under it, climb good face cracks to the right, to a short left-facing offwidth. Step left at its top onto loose ground and belay on a ledge or tower; this may be the top of the Becky chimney.
Continue up and left along ledges and corners to a ramp that trends left, and belay at the top of it.
Join the Honeymoon variation of the Snowpatch Route. Head up small offwidths and ramps to a small roof, go left onto ramps, and continue to the ridge crest.

review.changed: Wrote all 11 pitches. P6 length given as 30-40 m so omitted. No rappel stations described, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.12- and 11 pitches agree. Optional pitch splits suggested for P3 and P7.

pitch_detail.notes: Climb broken ledges to reach the corner. Mostly free climbing at about 5.10-.
Follow the corner, mostly on aid, until you can transfer to a crack in the right wall. The belay is an exposed seat, where two ropes hang fixed to the glacier.
Climb a steep crack using knifeblades, then a bolt ladder across a bulge, finishing on a ledge or alcove.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches the text describes; stored count is 5, and the upper pitches are not described. No aid grades per pitch, so none written.
review.other_findings: Source is incomplete (author recalls details only vaguely); pitches 4-5 unwritten.

pitch_detail.notes: Step across the moat, which gets harder later in the season. Climb double cracks and a flake for about 10 m, then trend right easily up the big scoop. Build a gear anchor before it steepens, where good foot ledges exist.
The thin corner crack carries on up the scoop to a bolted belay at a good stance.

Pull through a small overhang in the corner above to a stance, then go left and up a shallow corner that faces left, until an easy ramp leads right again. Traverse the ramp, hand-traversing flakes, to a bolted station under a long corner facing left.

A tips-width corner leads into a stemming section. Clip the bolt and face-climb left to the arete; avoid clipping up to the bolted station above right, which forces about 3 m of downclimbing. From the arete stance, return up and right into the corner and pass one more tips crux to a bolted station on a good ledge.

Two body lengths of fists lead to a small overhang, where a #5 cam helps the crux move. Skip the obvious corner: spot a bolt overhead, climb to it and shift left to a nicer corner system, which ends at a 4th-class ledge. Traverse that up and left to a bolt below a groove (the start of Minotaur) and keep going five metres to a two-bolt station under a good-looking flake.
Go up the flake, hand-traverse it leftward until it is a walkable ledge, then at the far end go up and left through small overlaps, face-climb left and back right to a bolted station.

Here you meet the roof section of Deus Ex Machina. Shift left from the belay and climb face holds up a small corner on the right, then slide left into the main corner and follow it through several small roofs to the bolted anchor.

Climb five metres of the right crack to a ledge, step left into an easy wide corner and follow it to a good ledge. Another short corner with a couple of tricky moves leads to a gear belay on a further good ledge. Rope drag is a factor, so consider splitting the pitch.

A superb pitch of twin cracks protected by gear and three bolts. A fixed wire and a bolt at a small stance give an optional belay, but linking the next 30 m of sustained 5.10 to a great ledge with a bolted belay is better.
Take the finger crack up and right, then a stretch of fist crack. Two bolts lead left across to a ledge system with a two-bolt anchor at its far left end.

A clean corner goes from hands to fists to offwidth. When it is too wide for a #5, two body lengths of easy laybacking pass the wide part to easier ground. Continue up the groove to a two-bolt station under black overhangs.
Climb through overhangs with some great, unlikely moves and belay at a good ledge. Linking with the next pitch is not recommended.
Follow the crack up and left to a big ledge. A little dirty for now.

review.changed: Wrote all 13 pitches with grade, length, anchors where stated. The modern descent is rappelling Minotaur Direct; the partial rappel list quoted is a different, older descent mixed with scrambling, not a clean station table, so none written.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.11d, but the highest pitch grade stated is 5.11+; the stated total pitch length is about 555 m vs stored 549.

pitch_detail.notes: The entry pitch follows the existing Tower Arete line. A direct line on another thin seam to the left looks possible.
A long pitch wanders over ledges, blocks and flowers toward the dihedral on the left. Stop under a gleaming right-facing corner that is closed up.

Starting beneath the blank corner, look a little to the right and climb about 15 ft to an overlap with flaky holds. You end up on a pillar. A bit spicy, yet the holds are just good enough, finishing in a granite hueco.
A beautiful left-facing widening hand crack runs parallel to the original dihedral system. Belay at a stance suitable for descending.
A longer pitch up the next wide hands and fists splitter, burly, finishing by stepping left to a stance back in the dihedral system.

The direct line is blocked by a flaring crack and rotten rock, so veer sharply right, foot-traversing, then climb a sketchy layback flake. Rope drag is heavy. Step hard right again onto moderate terrain, gain the ridge, and follow blocks to the summit.

review.changed: Wrote 6 pitches (P1 is thin, only its line and grade). No lengths or bolts stated.
review.other_findings: Stored 5.12a/b R; the text rates the hardest pitch 5.12 R.

pitch_detail.notes: A stiff, short pitch rises from the snow to a block at the notch's low point. Set your belay at the base of the pitch away from the line of rockfall. The top-of-notch block is an awkward stance, where you can sit in your harness or straddle the ridge.
Continue astride the ridge, taking care climbing the gendarme, and belay off its top.

Follow the ridge and up loose blocks. A horn just south of the summit is bypassed on its east side. A decent block just short of the summit on the south side makes a belay. One 60 m rappel returns you to the snow slope.

review.changed: Wrote 3 pitches matching stored count. No grades per pitch. The single 60 m rappel is a one-line description, no station list, so no rappel table.
review.other_findings: Route is serious: rotten ridge, loose blocks; snow cover helps on the choss slopes below the summit.

skip_reasons.bc_slesse_mountain_west_pillar: Text describes only the route line and that pitch 2 (flaring crack to a roof) is the crux; no pitch-by-pitch description.
skip_reasons.bc_pigeon_feathers_wild_fire: only 5 of 11 pitches described and parties turned back after P4
